title: Arithmetic sequences and fixed increments
transcript: In an arithmetic sequence each new term adds the same difference. The term number counts entries, but the changes happen in the gaps between entries. For a total of several terms, pair values from the two ends. Their sums are equal.

AMC practice can hide a fixed increment in a seating plan, a stack or a pattern of growing figures. Check whether the differences are constant. A Rossmoyne style question may need a total without listing every term. Pairing gives a short calculation and a reason.
A list starts at four and increases by three each time. What are the first four terms? Count the starting number as the first term.
Add three three times after the starting value. That produces four, seven, ten and thirteen. There are four terms but only three gaps. The fixed step is the size of each gap.
A sequence has first term four and common difference three. What is term fourteen? Work out how many gaps separate that term from the first.

Term fourteen is thirteen steps beyond term one. The total increase is that number of steps times three. Add the first term. The requested term is forty-three. Check the rule would give four at term one.
A theatre section starts with four seats in its first row. Each new row contains three more than the row before it. There are twelve rows. Find the total number of seats.

The last row contains thirty-seven, after eleven increases. Pair the first row with the last. Every pair totals forty-one. Moving inward adds three to one end and removes three from the other. There are six pairs. Multiply by the common pair total to get two hundred and forty-six seats.

A check is to imagine the rows redistributed evenly. The mean of the first and last values is the mean row length. Multiplying that mean by all twelve rows gives the same total, two hundred and forty-six seats.

The starting value occupies term one. A later position needs one fewer step than its term number. If the step changes, arithmetic-sequence formulas no longer apply. Check the first few differences before summing.

Write the first term and common difference. For a particular term, count the gaps before multiplying. For a sum, check the last term and whether there is an unpaired centre. Pair opposite ends to verify the total.
